candidates.statement: Use of human- and animal-derived materials during product manufacturing may increase risks of 72 infectious disease transmission, and raises potential safety concerns, such as the possible 73 introduction of adventitious agents or other impurities into CGT products and TEMPs. Thus, 74 human- and animal-derived materials should be thoroughly characterized and described in your 75 regulatory submission. 76

candidates.statement: Human- and animal-derived materials increase the risk of introducing adventitious 129 agents, including viruses, parasites, bacteria, mycoplasma and agent(s) responsible for 130 transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs). If the manufacturing process of the 131 material includes steps that you rely upon to remove or inactivate potential infectious 132 contaminants from these materials, the regulatory submission should describe how the 133 manufacturing method for the material has been demonstrated to remove adventitious 134 agents. For example, you or the manufacturer of the material should qualify the 135 processing methods and any sterilization techniques used in material manufacture for 136 their ability to inactivate and remove infectious contaminants. If removal or inactivation 137 of the potential infectious contaminant cannot be demonstrated, such as agent(s) 138 responsible for TSEs, careful source material selection may be a risk mitigation strategy. 139
candidates.context: A. Adventitious Agents 127 The introduction into a manufacturing facility of a material that is contaminated with an 141 adventitious agent carries the risk of contaminating other products or infecting personnel 142 with the adventitious agent. For example, a mycoplasma contamination introduced via a 143 material can be spread to equipment and personnel. We recommend that you develop 144 procedures to ensure that contaminated materials do not compromise the quality and 145 purity of the product. In cases where adventitious agent testing or examination of 146 materials is pending at the time of receipt, quarantining the material until completion of 147 the testing must be part of an overall current good manufacturing practice (CGMP)- 148 compliant strategy under our CGMP regulations (21 CFR 211.82). 6

candidates.statement: CGMP regulations require identity testing of materials, and specific tests should be used 181 if they are available (21 CFR 211.84(d)(1)). Although the production of an 182 investigational drug for use in a phase 1 study is exempt from compliance with the 183 regulations in 21 CFR part 211 (21 CFR 210.2(c)), manufacturers must follow statutory 184 CGMP required under section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act 7 , and you should consider 185 implementing identity testing, even during phase 1 clinical investigations, in order to 186 minimize any unintended compromise to product safety or quality. For example, if there 187 is a similar material being used in the same facility, such as similar types of sera or media 188 supplements, it is important to verify material identity. For phase 1 investigations, you 189 should establish written procedures describing the handling, review, acceptance, and 190 control of materials used in the manufacture (Ref. 5). 191 Materials must be tested for conformance with all appropriate written specifications for 192 purity, strength, and quality; or alternatively you may rely on a report of analysis from 193 the supplier, provided that the manufacturer conducts at least one specific identify test 194 and establishes the reliability of the supplier’s analyses (21 CFR 211.84(d)(2)). Your risk 195 analysis should determine whether it is adequate to rely on testing performed by the 196 supplier and reported on a COA, or whether you should also perform additional tests 197 prior to acceptance of a material. candidates.statement: Human-derived materials are frequently obtained from blood and blood components, 9 including 238 Source Plasma. Source Plasma is the fluid portion of human blood collected by plasmapheresis 239 and intended as a source material for further manufacturing use. The definition excludes single- 240 donor plasma products intended for intravenous use (21 CFR 640.60). Some materials used in 241 manufacturing CGT products and TEMPs can be derived from multiple types of donated source 242 material. For example, human AB serum can be manufactured from whole blood, single-donor 243 plasma, or Source Plasma. The testing requirements for Source Plasma are different than those 244 for whole blood and plasma. For example, Source Plasma, which is intended solely for further 245 manufacturing use, is not required to be tested for human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV), West 246 Nile virus (WNV), and Chagas disease (21 CFR 610.40 (a)(2)(ii)) and the requirements for 247 testing Source Plasma donations for syphilis differ from the requirements for testing donations of 248 other blood components for syphilis (see 21 CFR 610.40 (a)(2)(i) and 21 CFR 640.65(b)(2)) (see 249 section IV.C.2 of this guidance). Thus, your regulatory submission should document the type of 250 donated source material (e.g., blood, plasma, platelets, Source Plasma, etc.) used to manufacture 251 the human-derived material. 252

candidates.statement: In general, TSE may be transmitted between humans, and thus, human-derived materials 278 pose a risk of TSE transmission. Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) and variant 279 Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (vCJD) are relevant transfusion-transmitted infections (RTTI) 280 diseases under 21 CFR 603.3(h) and blood establishments must assess a donor’s medical 281 history to identify risk factors closely associated with an RTTI. The guidance titled, 282 “Recommendations to Reduce the Possible Risk of Transmission of Creutzfeldt-Jakob 283 Disease and Variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease by Blood and Blood Components,” dated 284 May 2022 (CJD guidance) (Ref. 6), outlines the possible risks associated with the 285 transmission of CJD (a type of TSE) and vCJD by blood and blood components and 286 provides donor deferral recommendations. We recommend that human blood-derived 287 materials are derived from donations collected at blood establishments that follow the 288 recommendations in the CJD guidance. 289

candidates.statement: Human blood-derived proteins can be added to culture media. For example, 365 transferrin is a blood protein that is used as a media additive to minimize 366 oxidative stress by chelating iron. It is often added as a supplement to “serum- 367 free,” “serum-reduced,” “xeno-free” or other supplemented cell culture media. 368 For example, although there are recombinant forms of transferrin, commercial 369 media formulations often contain human plasma-derived transferrin. The 370 presence of a human-derived protein in cell culture media, such as transferrin or 371 HSA, may not be immediately apparent on the COA supplied for the medium. 372 Therefore, you should document in the submissions to FDA the presence of 373 human-derived proteins in all media used to manufacture CGT products and 374 TEMPs. Moreover, you should include information to document conformance to 375 donor testing requirements specified in 21 CFR 610.40 and that the human- 376 derived material has been manufactured using procedures that have been validated 377 to clear or inactivate human adventitious agents. Manufacturers of culture media 378 used in manufacture of CGT or TEMP products who wish to provide confidential 379 information about their media to FDA should submit a Type II drug master file 380 (DMF) to the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER). If a MF is 381 available for a material, a letter of authorization that authorizes the 382 cross-reference of information in the MF and that is signed by the person who 383 submitted the cross-referenced information should be included in an IND 384 submission (21 CFR 312.23(b)). 385

candidates.statement: Human-derived feeder and bystander cells and cell-derived particles (e.g., extracellular vesicles, 391 exosomes, secreted proteins) may be used to propagate human cells during manufacturing of 392 CGT products and TEMPs. Some examples include immortalized feeder cells, allogeneic cells 393 irradiated at high dose to yield cell particles, and cells that have been genetically modified to 394 express certain stimulatory proteins. Ascertaining complete absence of residual cells from the 395 final product is technically challenging, and the feeder or bystander cells and cell-derived 396 particles may thus be present in the DS and DP as impurities. Moreover, feeder or bystander 397 cells and cell-derived particles are frequently used in culture with CGT products or TEMPs for 398 prolonged periods of time, which may increase the risk of transmission of adventitious agents 399 from the feeder cells to cells in the final product. For these reasons, we recommend that feeder 400 and bystander cells and cell particles derived from human cells should be derived from donors 401 who meet the eligibility criteria in 21 CFR part 1271, subpart C. We also recommend that feeder 402 and bystander cell banks are tested for sterility, mycoplasma, relevant human adventitious 403

candidates.statement: The Cell Therapy CMC Guidance and Gene Therapy CMC Guidance outline the 457 concerns associated with porcine materials (Refs. 2 and 3). Trypsin is a commonly used 458 material that is derived from pigs. We recommend that you use a trypsin alternative that 459 is free of porcine-derived materials, if it is appropriate for your specific application. For 460 safety testing of porcine materials, we recommend testing consistent with the testing for 461 ingredients of animal origin used for production of biologics described in 9 CFR 113.53 462 and consistent with the test methods outlined in 9 CFR 113.47. Documentation should 463 also demonstrate that the porcine-derived materials are tested for porcine circovirus 464 (PCV) 1 and 2 and porcine parvovirus. 465

candidates.statement: Cytokines and other proteins may be manufactured using insect cell lines. Insect-derived 469 materials may introduce rhabdovirus (Ref. 11) and spiroplasma (Ref. 12). Thus, 470 materials made in insect cell lines should be tested for rhabdovirus, mycoplasma, and 471 spiroplasma. You should submit additional information regarding any additional specific 472 adventitious viral agent testing that was performed on the material and/or cell line and 473 describe any viral clearance/reduction procedures that were performed during purification 474 of the material. 475

candidates.statement: You should closely examine the formulations of media and enzymes, because the use of 479 animal-derived reagents may not be readily apparent on the COA. For instance, chicken 480 egg-derived lecithin is a media additive, and some enzymes may be derived from 481 crustaceans. Moreover, non-mammalian animal-derived materials may be used in 482 fermentation of bacteria used to produce enzymes. If specific pathogen-free animals are 483 available, we recommend that materials be sourced from specific pathogen-free animals. 484 Your regulatory submission should contain information regarding any testing for relevant 485 animal pathogens, including the acceptance criteria for any animal tissues that are used in 486 the manufacture of the material. You should also submit the results of testing and release 487 criteria for animal tissues used in TEMPs (e.g., parts of DS or DP of the TEMP derived 488 from animal source such as porcine-derived extracellular matrix). You should perform a 489 risk assessment and document any viral inactivation steps present in the manufacture of 490 the animal-derived material. 491

candidates.statement: The use of materials derived from animal tissues and organs in TEMPs poses the risk of 523 transmission of animal adventitious agents. For decellularized tissue matrix, you should provide 524 evidence of the absence of cellular material, both viable and non-viable, document the methods 525 of decellularization and terminal sterilization (if applicable), and document the sterilization 526 assurance level. If you are relying on decellularization and sterilization methods for viral 527 inactivation, you should submit data demonstrating the viral inactivation properties associated 528 with the manufacturing and/or sterilization processes. The results of your viral inactivation 529 studies should include the sum of the log10 reduction in virus from selected processing steps and 530 sterilization process(es) (i.e., the overall virus reduction factor). 531
candidates.context: TEMPs commonly incorporate cells and scaffolds. Manufacturing of TEMPs may include 510 animal- and human-derived materials, such as media, media supplements, and scaffolds. Unlike 511 other types of materials used in product manufacturing, scaffolds may be an integral part of the 512 final formulated TEMP that contributes to the intended therapeutic effect. The general concepts 513 outlined in this guidance for animal- and human-derived materials apply to TEMPs, including 514 those that may become a part of a DS or DP. candidates.statement: We recommend communication with the Office of Therapeutic Products (OTP) in CBER early in 542 product development, before submission of an IND, via pre-IND (Ref. 15) or INitial Targeted 543 Engagement for Regulatory Advice on CBER producTs (INTERACT) meeting request. 13 In 544 your pre-IND or INTERACT meeting request, we recommend that you include specific 545 questions about human- and animal-derived material safety and quality and provide sufficient 546 background information to support their safety and quality, as outlined above, in this section of 547 the guidance. Changes to materials for products under an IND or a biologics license application 548 (BLA) should be reported in an IND amendment or BLA supplement, respectively. 549
